W.P.(CRL.) NO.160 OF 2024:
The petitioner herein has filed this Writ Petition under
Article 32 of the Constitution of India seeking the following reliefs:
“a. issue an appropriate writ of Mandamus, order or
direction clubbing/ transferring the FIR No.427 dated

registered at Police Station Schana distt S.A.S. Nagar
Mohali  in  the  State  of  Punjab,  FIR

406, 420, 114 IPC registered at Police Station
Dhanera distt. Banaskanta in the State of Gujarat
and FIR NO.0814/2023 dated 04.07.2023 under
Section 66(c), 65(d) of I.T.Act under Sections 419,
420 of IPC registered at Police Station Whitefield CEN
Crime Distt. Bengaluru city in the State of Karnataka
to the State of Maharashtra where the first FIR
No.387 dated 26.06.2023 under Section 34,420
1

--- Page 32 ---
Police Station Amboli distt. Brihanmumbai had been
registered and is currently under investigation, in the
interest of justice.
b. Pass such other orders and further orders as may
be deemed necessary on the facts and in the
circumstances of the case.”
2. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner; learned

5. Learned counsel contended that offences have been
registered against the petitioner herein presently in as many as
four States; that possibly offences may be registered in other
States also. Moreover, the offences which are registered in these
four States are in different jurisdictions and within the States of
Karnataka and Punjab, the offences are registered within multiple
territorial Districts; that investigations as against those offences
are pending independent of each other. 
3

--- Page 34 ---
6. The grievance of the petitioner is that as an accused, the
petitioner has to face these investigations in multiple States and
in different territorial jurisdictions within the States of Karantaka
and Gujarat.
7. Learned counsel for the petitioner therefore, submitted that
the petitioner has sought a Writ of Mandamus and for issuance of
a direction for clubbing of all the offences pending investigation
before different territorial jurisdictions in different States by
transferring those FIRs to any one jurisdiction in a State.
8. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the rights
of the accused would have to be considered inasmuch as the
petitioner, being a lady, cannot be exposed to investigation in
multiple jurisdictions and in different States viz., Maharashtra,
Karnataka, Gujarat and Punjab. Hence, the prayer sought for by
the petitioner may be granted. In this regard, reliance was placed
on a judgment of this Court in Amit Katyal and another vs.
State of Haryana and another (2026 SCC ONLINE SC 890).
9. Per contra , learned standing counsel for the respondent(s)-
States submitted in unison that the prayers sought for by the
petitioner herein cannot be granted in as much as each State is
4

--- Page 35 ---
carrying out investigation depending on the local laws as well as
under the provisions of the Indian Penal Code. For instance, in
the State of Maharashtra and Gujarat, the Protection of Interest of
Depositors Act of the respective States which are State
Legislations have also been invoked by the complainants and the
FIRs have been registered under those provisions and hence, the
respective States have to investigate the offences not only under
the provisions of the IPC but also the State enactments regarding
the Protection of Interest of Depositors Act. They therefore,
contended that if at all this Court is inclined to grant any relief,
then the multiple FIRs which have been registered within the
States may be clubbed to one Jurisdiction and in that regard,
liberty may be reserved to the petitioner herein to move
appropriate forum in accordance with law.
10. We have considered the submissions advanced at the bar in
light of the judgments of this Court in the case of Amandeep
Singh Saran vs. State of Delhi (2023 SCC Online SC 1851) ;
Radhey  Shyam  vs.  State  of  Haryana  disposed  of  on
12.05.2022 WP (Crl.) No.75 of 2020 which has been considered
in Amandeep Singh Saran ;  and  Odela Satyam vs. State of
5

--- Page 36 ---
Telangana and others passed in Writ Petition (Criminal)
No.20 of 2025 reported in (2025 SCC Online SC 2018).
11. We take note of the fact that in the instant case the
petitioner herein is facing investigation under the provisions of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) in as many as four States and

     (REPORTABLE)
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
    CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.________ OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(Criminal) No.16000/2025)
SANDEEP JHAVERI                                   Appellant(s)
                              VERSUS
STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ANR.                      Respondent(s)
      O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Under the impugned order, the
High Court has rejected the appellant’s
prayer  for  quashing  of  the  FIR,  dated
05.07.2023,  bearing  No.  539  of  2023
registered with Santacruz Police Station,
District Greater Mumbai for the offence
punishable under Section 420 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860.
3. The  respondent  no.2,  Sameer
Kishore  Ganatra,  alleged  that  the
appellant  induced  him  to  invest,  in
several chunks, a cumulative amount of Rs.
28,00,000/-  promising  good  returns,  in
Crypto Currency, however, later on, the

--- Page 45 ---
2
appellant refused to return the amount of
Rs. 28,00,000/-.
4. After  registration  of  the
subject FIR, appellant’s anticipatory bail
was rejected on 09.02.2024 and thereafter,
the appellant was arrested on 15.02.2024.
A consent deed was executed between the
appellant’s  wife, Smt.Rachna  Zaveri  and
respondent  no.2/  complainant,   Sameer
Kishore  Ganatra, on  27.02.2024  wherein,
the respondent no.2 agreed for quashing of
the subject FIR if, the appellant pays
Rs.18,00,000/- to him. In accordance with
the  terms  of  the  consent  deed,  the
appellant paid Rs.15 lakhs to respondent
no.2  on  28.02.2024  and  thereafter,
appellant’s bail petition/ application was
considered  by  the  Additional  Sessions
Judge  at  Greater  Bombay  wherein  the
respondent no.2 appeared and endorsed the
terms  of  consent  and  also  filed  an
affidavit basis which, the appellant was
released on bail.
5. Thereafter, the balance sum of
Rs.3 lakhs was also paid to respondent

--- Page 46 ---
3
no.2  vide  receipt  dated  10.03.2024
(annexure P-5).
6. While being so, the appellant
preferred a quashing petition in the High
Court which has now been rejected under
the impugned order solely on the ground
that the consent deed was recorded between
the appellant’s wife and respondent no.2
and also that the charge sheet has already
been  filed.  Therefore,  no  case  for
quashment  is  made  out  as  there  is  no
validly executed consent terms between the
parties.
7. Reiterating  the  submission
made  before the High Court, Mr. Gaurav
Agarwal, learned senior counsel appearing
for the appellant would submit that once
the  respondent  no.2  has  agreed  for
quashing of the subject FIR upon receipt
of Rs.18 lakhs, the High Court should have
exercised  powers  under  Section  482  of
Cr.P.C. for quashing of the FIR and the
reasons assigned for not exercising such
powers are not proper.

--- Page 47 ---
4
8. Per  contra,  learned  counsel
appearing for respondent no.2 would submit
that in the teeth of the consent deed
executed  on  27.02.2024,  it  would  be
apparent that the same is not signed by
the  appellant.  Therefore,  any  agreement
between  the  appellant’s  wife  and
respondent no.2, cannot be considered as a
valid compromise in terms of Section 320
of  Cr.P.C.  Therefore,  there  being  no
compromise in the eye of law, the High
Court has rightly refused to quash the
subject FIR. Moreover, since charge sheet
has already been filed, now the subject
FIR has no independent existence and the
High  Court  is  absolutely  justified  in
refusing  prayer  for  quashing  of  the
subject FIR.
9. Having heard learned counsel
for the parties, we are of the considered
view that the High Court ought to have
exercised  its  inherent  powers  under
Section 482 of Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR
for reasons more than one.
10. Firstly, the terms of consent, as

--- Page 48 ---
5
recorded between the appellant’s wife and
respondent  no.2,  clearly  records  the
following;
  CONSENT TERMS 
1.  That the Consent Terms are
being entered into between the
Applicant's wife Rachna Sandeep
Jhaveri on behalf of Mr. Sandeep
Jhaveri (The Applicant) and Mr.
Samir Kishore Ganatra (The First
Informant).
2. Whereas both the First
Informant  as  well  as  the
Applicant  hereby  declare  that
the  disputes  and  differences
between  them  have  been
reconciled and they have arrived
at these consent terms.
3. Whereas  the  First
Informant,  Mr.  Samir  Kishore
Ganatra,  had  filed  an  F.I.R.
bearing C.R. No. 539 of 2023
(The said F.I.R) which came to
be  registered  with  Santacruz
Police Station on 05/07/2023 for
the  offence  punishable  under
Section 420 of the Indian Penal
Code and that by the way of the
said F.I.R. bearing No. 539 of
2023  the  First  informant  had
alleged that the Applicant had
allegedly  cheated  him  for  an
amount  of  Rs.  28,00,000/-
(Rupees Twenty Eight Lakhs).
4. Whereas, the Applicant's
wife Mrs. Rachna Sandeep Jhaveri
has  assured  that  she  will
reimburse  the  First  informant

--- Page 49 ---
6
with an amount of Rs, 18,00,000-
(Rupees Eighteen Lakhs Only) and
hereby in the view of the same
the First Informant is willing
to withdraw all the allegations
made against the Applicant in
the said F.I.R and which were
made  during  the  course  of
consequential proceedings.
NOW THESE TERMS WITHNESSTH AS
UNDER:
I. That  the  Org.
Complainant  will  give  his
consent in the quashing of the
F.I.R  bearing  C.R  No.  539
registered with Santacruz Police
Station  and  will  oblige  with
proceeding  of  the  matter
pertaining to the quashing of
the F.I.R bearing C.R No. 539 of
2023 dated 05/07/2023 registered
with  Santacruz  Police  Station
and First Informant will appear
as and when required/ necessary
for the same.
II. In view of the amicable
settlement  of  disputes  and
differences, the First Informant
shall  give  his  consent  to
withdraw  all  the  allegations
against the Applicant.
III. That the Applicant has
agreed  to  settle  all  their
disputes and the Applicant has
agreed to give an of an amount

--- Page 50 ---
7
of  Rs.  18.00,000/-  (Rupees
Eighteen Lakhs Only) as a form
of  full  and  final  settlement
amount.”
Having  so  agreed  and  accorded
consent for quashing of the subject FIR,
the respondent no.2 thereafter, appeared
before the Court of Additional Sessions
Judge at Greater Bombay on 01.03.2024 and
endorsed  the  consent  terms  and
categorically submitted that he wants to
withdraw the allegations levelled against
the appellant. Even if the said concession
was  at  the  time  of  consideration  for
appellant’s prayer for grant of bail, the
fact remains that respondent no.2 not only
consented for appellant’s release on bail
but also stated before the Court that he
wants to withdraw the allegations levelled
against the appellant. He has also filed
an  affidavit  before  the  said  Court  in
which he agreed and endorsed the terms of
consent deed.
11. Secondly,  the  High  Court’s
observation that there  is  no  valid
execution of terms of consent between the
parties, would not deter the Court for

--- Page 51 ---
8
exercising  powers  under  Section  482  of
Cr.P.C. inasmuch as the appellant still
agrees with the terms of consent and he
abides  by  his  wife’s  agreement  to  the
terms of the consent deed.
12. It is not that the informant/
respondent  no.2  has  not  signed  the
documents.  If  the  informant/  respondent
no.2 has signed the consent terms and the
appellant is still abiding by the same, it
is not a case where there is no valid
consent between the parties.
13. It is also to be seen that in
terms of the consent, the appellant has
already received a sum of Rs.15 lakhs on
28.02.2024 and the balance sum of Rs.3
lakhs on 10.03.2024. Thus, upon receipt of
the  entire  settlement  amount  of  Rs  18
lakhs,  the  consent  terms  were  fully
complied with leaving nothing more to be
done by the parties.
14. Once the terms of consent have
been fully complied with by the appellant,
initially through his wife and thereafter,
by himself paying the balance sum of Rs.3

--- Page 52 ---
9
lakhs,  the  High  Court  ought  to  have
appreciated the entire gamut of facts and
the  chain  of  events  to  cull  out  the
reasoning that on the date of execution of
the terms of consent deed, the parties
were  truly  and  sincerely  willing  to
compound  the  offence  and  thereafter,
respondent no.2 has reiterated the terms
of  consent  deed  during  the  Court’s
proceedings  when  the  appellant’s  bail
petition was considered on 01.03.2024.
15. In  view  of  the  above
discussion, we are of the considered view
that the appellant has made out a case for
quashing of the subject FIR in terms of
the terms of consent entered between the
parties.
16. Accordingly, the subject FIR
bearing No. 539 of 2023 registered with
Santacruz Police Station, District Greater
Mumbai, is quashed.

--- Page 53 ---
10
17. The  appeal  is  allowed
accordingly.

UNION OF INDIA AND

WITH 
 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 182 OF 2025 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. Heard in part 
2. This Court, vide order dated 3 rd September, 
2026, upon consideration of the Status Report dated 
31st August, 2026 submitted by the High -Powered 
Committee for Reform and Governance of Open 
Correctional Institutions 1 and the submissions 
advanced by the learned Amicus Curiae , issued 
certain directions considered necessary to facilitate 
 
1 Hereinafter, being referred to as “High-Powered Committee”. 

--- Page 66 ---
2 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
the effective and smooth functioning of the High -
Powered Committee and to advance the reformative 
and rehabilitative objectives underlying the 
establishment of Open Correctional Institutions. The 
directions, inter alia, required effective representation 
of the concerned States and Union Territories before 
the High -Powered Committee, filing of requisite 
compliance affidavits in respect of the rights of 
prisoners with disabilities, and nomination by the 
Ministry of Home Affairs of an officer to attend to the 
administrative requirements of the High-Powered 
Committee and participate in its ongoing meetings.  
3. The matter was thereafter directed to be listed 
on 29 th September, 2026, for consideration of the 
further Status Report to be submitted by the High -
Powered Committee, indicating the progress made 
and the recommendations, if any, formulated by it in 
furtherance of the mandate entrusted to it by the 
judgment date d 26 th February, 2026 in Suhas 
Chakma v. Union of India and the judgment dated 
21st April, 2026 in Sathyan Naravoor v. Union of 
India. 
4. When the matter was taken up for hearing on 
29th September, 2026, the learned Amicus Curiae  

--- Page 67 ---
3 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
placed a note indicating the status of compliance with 
the directions contained in the order dated 3 rd 
September, 2026. The learned Amicus Curiae pointed 
out that,  notwithstanding the aforesaid directions, 
several States and Union Territories had not yet 
complied with the requirement of ensuring effective 
representation before the High -Powered Committee 
by the Secretaries of the Department of Social Justice 
and Empowerment/Department of Social Welfare, as 
the case may be, or their nominees not below the 
rank of Additional Secretary.2 It was further brought 
to the notice of the Court that the requisite 
compliance affidavits concerning the rights of 
prisoners with disabilities had also not been filed by 
the States and Union Territories identified in the note 
placed before the Court.3 
 
2 States of Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Goa, Gujarat, 
Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, 
Manipur, Mizoram, Punjab, Telangana and West Bengal, and the Union 
Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh,  Dadra and 
Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Delhi, Ladakh, Lakshadweep and 
Jammu and Kashmir. 
3 States of Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Goa, 
Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, 
Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and West Bengal, and the Union 
Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra an d 
Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Delhi, Jammu and Kashmir, 
Lakshadweep and Ladakh. 

--- Page 68 ---
4 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
5. The learned Amicus Curiae further pointed out 
that the direction requiring the Ministry of Home 
Affairs, Government of India, to nominate an officer 
not below the rank of Joint Secretary to attend to the 
administrative requirements of the High -Powered 
Committee and to participate in its ongoing meetings 
had also not been complied with. It was submitted 
that the absence of such coordination, coupled with 
the continued non -compliance by the concerned 
States and Union Territories, was affecting the 
effective discharge of the mandate entrusted to the 
High-Powered Committee by this Court.  
6. At the same time, the learned Amicus Curiae  
pointed out  that the High -Powered Committee had 
proceeded with the substantive work entrusted to it 
and had constituted sub -committees to examine, 
inter alia , the conceptual framework of Open 
Correctional Institutions, eligibility criteria for 
transfer thereto, skill development, vocational 
training and education, revision of wages, inclusion 
of women in Open Correctional Institutions, and the 
treatment of prisoners with disabilities. It was 
submitted that, as part of the exercise of gathering 
comprehensive information necessary for the 

--- Page 69 ---
5 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
discharge of its mandate, questionnaires had been 
circulated to the concerned stakeholders, including 
judicial officers and the prison departments of the 
States and Union Territories, as also to released 
prisoners of Open Correctional Institutions and 
family members, besides in relation to the treatment 
of prisoners with disabilities.  
7. The learned Amicus Curiae submitted that the 
questionnaires were at various stages of finalisation 
and pilot testing and that the High -Powered 
Committee required further time to collect and 
analyse the requisite information from the States and 
Union Territories and, upon completion of the 
exercise, formulate its preliminary recommendations. 
The learned Amicus Curiae, accordingly, prayed that 
the matter be deferred to a later date so as to enable 
the High -Powered Committee  to place its progress 
and preliminary recommendations before the Court 
for consideration. 
8. Having regard to the concerns and deficiencies 
brought to our notice by the learned  Amicus Curiae, 
we deem it appropriate to reiterate the directions 
contained in paragraphs 8(A) and 8(B)  of the order 
dated 3rd September, 2026. The concerned States and 

--- Page 70 ---
6 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
Union Territories shall, therefore, ensure compliance 
with the said directions in their letter and spirit, 
including effective representation before the High -
Powered Committee of the Secretaries of the 
Department of Social Justice and 
Empowerment/Department of Social Welfare, as the 
case may be, or their nominees not below the rank of 
Additional Secretary, and the filing of the requisite 
compliance affidavits in respect of the rights of 
prisoners with disabilities.  Compliance as directed 
above shall be ensured within a period of one month 
from the date of this order. 
9. We further direct the Ministry of Home Affairs, 
Government of India, to ensure compliance with the 
direction contained in paragraph 8(C)  of the order 
dated 3rd September, 2026, by nominating an officer 
not below the rank of Joint Secretary to attend to the 
administrative requirements of the High -Powered 
Committee and to participate in its ongoing meetings. 
The officer so nominated shall, in particular, facilitate 
coordination between the High -Powered Committee 
and the concerned States and Union Territories and 
ensure that the requisite information, responses and 
compliance are furnished to the High-Powered 

--- Page 71 ---
7 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
Committee without avoidable delay. The nomination 
of the designated officer and compliance with the 
aforesaid directions shall be completed within a 
period of two weeks from the date of this order. 
10. A copy of this order, as also a copy of the order 
dated 3 rd September, 2026, shall be transmitted by 
the Registry to the Chief Secretaries of the States of 
Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, 
Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, 
Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Punjab, Rajasthan, 
Tamil Nadu, Telangana and West Bengal, and to the 
Administrators/Chief Secretaries, as the case may 
be, of the Union Territories of Andaman and Nicobar 
Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and 
Daman and Diu, Delhi, Jammu and Kashmir, 
Ladakh and Lakshadweep,  for ensuring compliance 
with the directions contained therein. A copy of both 
the orders shall also be transmitted to the Union 
Home Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, 
Government of India, who shall ensure compliance 
with the direction concerning the no mination of the 
designated officer and facilitate coordination with the 
States and Union Territories for the effective 

--- Page 72 ---
8 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
implementation of the directions issued by  this 
Court. 
11. It is made clear that the directions issued by 
this Court are required to be complied with within the 
time stipulated and that no further delay in their 
implementation shall be countenanced. In the event 
of continued or unexplained non -compliance by any 
State or Union Territory, this Court may be 
constrained to require the personal presence of the 
concerned Chief Secretary/Administrator, as the 
case may be, before this Court to explain the 
circumstances in which the directions of this Court 
have not been complied with. 
12. In view of  the nature and magnitude of the 
exercise being undertaken by the High -Powered 
Committee, including the collection and analysis of 
information from the States and Union Territories, 
the work being undertaken by its various sub -
committees and the formulation of its preliminary 
recommendations, we consid er it appropriate to 
grant the Committee a further period of three months 
to complete the aforesaid exercise and place before 
this Court its progress report and preliminary 
recommendations. The matter s shall accordingly be 

--- Page 73 ---
9 
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.(S.) 1082 OF 2020 
 
listed on 12th January, 2027 for consideration of the 
further Status Report and the recommendations  of 
the High-Powered Committee. 
13. List for further hearing on 12th January, 2027.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Permission to file Special Leave Petition is granted.
2. The instant Special Leave Petitions concern the elections for
the posts of Councillors/Members of the Municipal Corporations,
Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats in the State of Punjab. 
3. The Petitioners are associated with different National/State
Political Parties and have approached this court,  inter  alia ,
alleging that: (i) Members of the ruling party, police officials,
and unknown third-parties prevented them from submitting their
nomination  forms,  including  by  physical  assault,  tearing  of
clothes, and snatching of the nomination papers; (ii) The entire
nomination process was not recorded through audio-visual means,
despite the High Court’s directions; (iii) The elections for the
posts of Mayor, Senior Deputy Mayor, and Deputy Mayor were being
conducted by an incomplete quorum, as the elections for certain
wards were still pending; and (iv) The Respondents consequently
elected unopposed, ought to be restrained from being administered
the oath of office.
4. Vide our order dated 24.03.2025, noting that the disputed
questions of fact could not be determined by the High Court or this
Court in exercise of the writ jurisdiction, and that the issues
were causing uncertainty over the functioning of the elected
municipal bodies, we resolved to appoint, with the consent of the
parties, a former Judge of the High Court to conduct a Fact-Finding
Enquiry into the claims/counter-claims of the parties, limited to
4

--- Page 78 ---
the sub-judice constituencies. 
5. Accordingly, Hon’ble Ms. Justice Nirmaljit Kaur, former Judge
of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, was appointed as the one-
member  Fact-Finding  Commission  (in  short,  “the  Commission”).
Liberty to submit claims was limited to those who had approached
the  High  Court  or  this  Court  by  way  of  special  leave
petitions/intervenor applications. Further, the State Authorities
were permitted to raise objections and produce the relevant record
before the Commission.
6. The Commission has submitted its report dated 18.11.2025,
which was circulated to the counsel for the parties. 
7. As  per  the  report,  of  46  claim  petitions  filed  by  85
claimants,  4  were  withdrawn  and  2  were  rejected  as  non-
maintainable. Of the remaining 40 petitions, 33 concerned the
Municipal Corporation, Patiala, while 7 concerned Dharamkot and
Baghapurana in District Moga. The Commission examined affidavits,
official replies, videos/CCTV footage, photographs, voter registers
and voter lists, and recorded statements of Returning and Presiding
Officers, polling staff, police officers, civil officials, the
Election Observer and the claimants.
8. The principal finding of the Commission is of widespread
obstruction  during  the  nomination  process,  whereby  nomination
papers were snatched, torn or destroyed, and candidates were
assaulted,  detained  or  threatened.  Regarding  the  Municipal
Corporation, Patiala, the Commission found the elections in 13
wards, i.e. Ward Nos. 1, 12, 32, 33, 36, 41, 43, 44, 45, 48, 50,
51, and 52, vitiated because opposition candidates were prevented
5

--- Page 79 ---
from filing nominations. Similarly, in Ward Nos. 4, 6, 14, 16, 22,
26, 28, 37, 38, 40, 46, 53, 55 and 57, the elections were found
vitiated because particular opposition candidates were forcibly
excluded from contesting, even though the Commission could not
determine  whether  their  participation  would  have  changed  the
result. Ward No. 34 was also found vitiated, as one Gaurav Kumar
was prevented from filing his nomination. 
9. As regards polling malpractices in Patiala, the Commission
found serious evidence of bogus/multiple voting and intimidation in
Ward Nos. 15 and 58, sufficient to question the fairness of those
elections, though it did not find that the proven irregularities
necessarily altered the result. However, the allegations regarding
Ward Nos. 7, 18, and 19 were found not proved for want of evidence.
10. In Municipal Council, Dharamkot, the Commission found the
elections in Ward Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9 and 13 vitiated due to
forcible prevention of nominations, coercive withdrawal or wrongful
rejection. Similarly, in Municipal Council, Baghapurana, it found
the elections to all 15 wards vitiated as opposition candidates
were systematically prevented from filing nominations. 
11. In aggregate, the Commission found 50 ward elections to be
vitiated and deserving of being set aside (28 in District Patiala
and 22 in District Moga).
12. Mr. Kapil Sibal, learned senior counsel appearing for the
State of Punjab, fairly states that the State has no objection to
the acceptance of the recommendations made by the Commission. We
therefore accept the recommendations of the Commission and direct
that fresh elections be conducted in the relevant 50 wards. 
6

--- Page 80 ---
13. In order to ensure that re-elections are conducted in a free,
fair, and transparent manner, we issue the following directions:
i. The Chief Justice of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana is
requested  to  appoint,  within  one  week,  a  Monitoring
Committee comprising a retired Judge of the High Court of
Punjab  and  Haryana  to  oversee  the  entire  process  of
conducting the by-elections afresh from the issuance of the
election notification until the declaration of the results.
The re-election schedule shall be notified only after the
Monitoring Committee has been duly constituted. 
ii. The Chief Justice of the High Court is also requested to
nominate atleast two or three senior members of the Bar of
the High Court to act as ‘Observers’ in the re-election
process.  The  filing,  scrutiny/submission  of  nomination
forms,  allocation  of  symbols,  polling,  etc.  shall  be
videographed in the presence of the said Observers. The
recordings shall be duly preserved and handed over to the
Monitoring Committee.  
iii. The  State  of  Punjab  shall  furnish  to  the  Monitoring
Committee, before the filing of nominations begins, a ward-
wise list of the officers/officials deployed on election
duty. Further, the list of police officers on duty in the
rank of DSP and above shall also be furnished. 
7

--- Page 81 ---
iv. Any complaint concerning interference with, or obstruction
of, the re-election process by any person, including any
official, may be made to the Monitoring Committee, which
shall promptly enquire into it and, if it finds substance in
the complaint, submit a report to the Chief Justice of the
High Court, who is requested to take appropriate action on
the judicial side.
  
v. The honorarium payable to the Monitoring Committee as well
as the Observers shall be fixed by the Chief Justice of the
High  Court.  The  honorarium  as  well  as  the  incidental
expenses of the Monitoring Committee and the Observers shall
be borne by the Government of Punjab, which shall also
provide them with the necessary secretarial, transportation,
logistical, and security support. 
 
vi. Upon completion of the entire re-election process, a report
regarding the conduct of the same shall be submitted to the
Chief Justice of the High Court. The re-election process
shall be deemed to be completed only upon the Chief Justice
of the High Court being satisfied, on the basis of the
report submitted, that they were conducted in a free and
fair manner. Only upon recording such satisfaction shall the
results of the re-election be declared. 
vii. The entire process of re-election shall be completed within
8

--- Page 82 ---
6 weeks.    
14. The  instant  Special  Leave  Petitions  are  disposed  of
accordingly, along with all pending Interlocutory Applications
including application(s) for intervention/impleadment. We clarify
that this order, including the directions above, has been passed in
the peculiar facts of these cases and shall not constitute a
precedent for future by-elections. The Registry shall forthwith
communicate a copy of this order to the Chief Justice of the High
Court of Punjab and Haryana. 
15. We also take this opportunity to place on record our sincere
appreciation for Hon’ble Ms. Justice Nirmaljit Kaur, former Judge
of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, for conducting the Fact-
Finding Enquiry with remarkable diligence and objectivity. Her
comprehensive report, prepared after a painstaking examination of
voluminous  oral,  documentary,  and  video  evidence  has  greatly
assisted this Court in bringing a quietus to these disputes. 
(NITIN TALREJA)                             (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner(s) has placed on record a chart
containing list of 13 matters (writ petitions) in which the petitioners have not
been paid the stipend during their internships. Though the affidavit of the
National Medical Commission (NMC) would reflect that all the colleges have paid
the stipend, this chart reflects picture contrary to the said stand. Hence, the
counsel appearing for the NMC shall ascertain the factual position with
reference to the 13 writ petitions as reflect in the chart furnished and shall file
an affidavit with regard to factual position within two weeks from today.
2.  Learned counsel for the petitioner(s) would also submit that in the State of
Rajasthan, the amount having been sanctioned same is not being released for
the reason of there being no budgetary sanction. Learned counsel appearing for
the State of Rajasthan would seek time to take instructions in the matter.
3. We make it clear that the orders passed by this Court requires to be
implemented in letter and spirit and in the event of said amount as ordered to
be paid to the stipendiary undergraduates (Doctors), is not paid, the Secretary,
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of Rajasthan, shall appear in
person and show cause as to why proceedings should not be initiated for
violation of order passed by this Court.
4. Writ Petition (C) No.976/2025 is also ordered to be taken along with present
batch of petitions.
5. List after two weeks.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                          OF 2026 
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.7239 of 2026) 
 
 
 
Chittibarika Chandra Shekar & Ors.         ...Appellants 
 
 
Versus 
 
The State of Telangana & Anr.      ...Respondents 
 
 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
Leave granted. 
2. The allegation levelled against the six accused, who 
are the appellant s herein are under Section 306 read with 
Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). It is alleged 
that the 1st appellant was in love with the deceased and 
though they were not married, they were living together. On 
the refusal of the first appellant to marry his lover , she 
committed suicide is the case projected by the siblings of the 
deceased. 

--- Page 92 ---
Page 2 of 5 
 
 
3. The FIR is produced at Annexure P1, registered on the 
First Information Statement (FIS) of the sister of the deceased. 
It is the case of the 1st informant that she had called up the 
friend of the deceased a few days back since her sister was 
not picking up her telephone. She was informed that her 
sister had been living with the 1st appellant in his house. The 
elder sister of the 1st informant then went to the house of the 
1st appellant and brought the deceased back to their house. 
It is admitted that there was a consensual relationship and 
they were living together for three months in the house of the 
1st appellant. It is also admitted that their relationship was 
accepted by the family of the 1st appellant. In that 
circumstance it is difficult to comprehend as to why the 1st 
informant and her sister took the deceased away from the 1st 
appellant’s house. 
4. Be that as it may, the FIS continues with a narration that 
on the next day morning the deceased went out to work and 
in the evening the 1st appellant called the 1st informant asking 
her where to drop her younger sister. She asked the 1st 
appellant to bring her back to their house, but the deceased 
did not return. Later it is alleged that her sister called up the 

--- Page 93 ---
Page 3 of 5 
 
 
eldest sister and told her that the first appellant had refused 
to marry him and hence she is ending her life. 
5. The 2nd appellant is the father and the 6 th appellant is 
the mother of the 1 st appellant, the 3rd appellant is the sister 
of the 1st appellant and the 5th appellant is the person who is 
the proposed bridegroom of the 3 rd appellant and the 4 th 
appellant is a friend of the 1st appellant. The allegation is that 
the 4 th respondent spoke ill of the deceased to the 1st 
appellant, which made him withdraw from the marriage 
proposal. The 3 rd appellant also implored the 1 st appellant 
from continuing the relationship ; especially since the 5 th 
appellant had refused to marry her , if the 1 st appellant 
entered into a marriage with the deceased. The 2 nd and 6 th 
appellants, who are the parents of the 1 st appellant, also 
concurred with this view. This is the long and short of the 
instigation to drive the deceased to death by suicide. 
6. That the death was by suicide is unequivocally 
proved. It also happened in the house of the 1 st appellant. 
That the 1st appellant had a consensual relationship with the 
deceased for the last few months, is also admitted by the first 
informant. In that circumstance , it is not clear as to why the 
first informant took away the deceased from the house of the 

--- Page 94 ---
Page 4 of 5 
 
 
1st appellant. When a phone call came to the elde st sister 
from the deceased , she did not do anything to avert the 
suicide threatened. We are unable to find any instigation by 
the accused/appellants to drive the deceased  to death by 
suicide. It was neither intended nor can it be said to be 
abetment. At the worst , even if we fully believe what has 
been stated by the 1st informant, there was a refusal of 
marriage, which led to the wom an committing suicide. 
People react differently to situations and if a breakup ends up 
with suicide, it cannot always be termed an abetment to 
suicide. The refusal to marry was not with an intention to 
drive the woman to death by suicide nor can knowledge be 
attributed to the accused that on such refusal , she would 
commit suicide. 
7. We are unable to sustain the prosecution initiated 
against the accused on such frivolous allegations and we 
quash the proceedings in Sessions Case No.101 of 2024  
pending before the Learned IInd Additional Senior Civil  
Judge-cum-Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate , Medchal-
Malkajgiri District at Kushaiguda, Telangana. 
8. The accused/appellants, if in custody, shall be 
released forthwith, if not required in any other case.  If they 

--- Page 95 ---
Page 5 of 5 
 
 
are already on bail, then their bail bonds shall stand 
cancelled. 
9. The appeal stands disposed of. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
Criminal Appeal No(s).      /2026
@ SLP (Crl) No. 13293/2026
ANU ANIL NAIR                                Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF KERALA & ANR.                      Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns the judgment and order of the High Court
of Kerala at Ernakulam dated 10.06.2026 by which the High
Court has declined to quash the proceedings emanating from
Crime  No.706/2024  registered  at  P.S.  Kalamassery  under
Sections 354, 354(A)(1)(ii), 354B, 376, 509 and 451 of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  which  are  now  pending  as  C.P.
No.5/2025 in the Court of Judicial First Class Magistrate,
Kalamassery.
4. The appellant and the second respondent were formerly engaged
to get married. The marriage could not take place, and a
1

--- Page 120 ---
complaint came to be lodged at the instance of the second
respondent wherein it was alleged that she was sexually
exploited by the appellant. The parties, however, resolved
their differences and, ultimately, based on a compromise,
prayed  for  quashing  of  the  proceedings  by  invoking  the
inherent powers of the High Court.
5. The  High  Court  declined  the  prayer  of  quashing  of  the
proceedings on the ground that an offence concerning sexual
assault falls in the category of heinous offences which cannot
be quashed based on a compromise.
6. Aggrieved by the order of the High Court, this appeal has been
filed.
7. On  31.07.2026,  after  considering  the  submissions  of  the
learned counsel for the appellant, we had passed the following
order:
“1.  The  submission  of  the  learned
counsel for the petitioner is that the
prosecutrix  and  the  petitioner  were
formally  engaged  to  get  married.
However,  on  account  of  certain
differences  between  them  a  First
Information Report (FIR) was lodged by
the prosecutrix alleging sexual assault
on her by the petitioner at her house.
Later, the differences were resolved
and an affidavit was presented by the
prosecutirx  before  the  High  Court
agreeing for quashment of the FIR and
the consequential proceedings as they
2

--- Page 121 ---
were  instituted  on  account  of  some
misunderstanding between them. 
2.  Considering  the  nature  of  the
offences, the High Court declined the
prayer to quash the FIR.
3. The submission on behalf of the
petitioner is that this is not a case
of usual rape but it is a case of
alleged physical relationship between
two persons who were formally engaged
to get married and, therefore, basis a
settlement,  the  proceedings  can  be
quashed to ensure that there is no
abuse of the process of law. Moreover,
it is a case where the prosecutrix
herself would be the witness and if she
is not wiling to come forward, the
trial would be an exercise in futility.
4.  Issue  notice,  returnable  in  six
weeks.  5.  Notice  on  behalf  of
respondent no.2 has been accepted by
Mr.  Jogy  Scaria,  AOR  6.  In  the
meantime, further proceedings emanating
from FIR No.706/2024 dated 23.07.2024
registered  at  P.S.  Kalamassery,
District Ernakulum City, Kerala shall
remain stayed.”
8.  Pursuant to the above order, the respondents are represented.
9.   The second respondent, who happens to be the complainant, is
represented through her Counsel.
3

--- Page 122 ---
10. The learned counsel representing the second respondent
submits that he would have no objection if the proceedings are
quashed on the basis of the compromise between the parties.
11. Having regard to the background facts of the case and the
relationship between the parties prior to the alleged incident
of sexual assault, we are of the view that this is a peculiar
case which cannot be equated with a case of sexual assault
simpliciter. Here the parties were engaged to get married and
during that relationship some incident occurred which was
reported.
12. In such circumstances, when the parties have resolved
their  differences  and  have  prayed  for  quashing  of  the
proceedings, no useful purpose would be served by continuing
those proceedings particularly when the relationship of the
parties permitted them to be in company of each other. We,
therefore, deem it appropriate to invoke our powers under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India and quash the
proceedings emanating from Crime No. 706/2024(supra).
13. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed. The order of the
High  Court  dated  10.06.2026  is  hereby  set  aside.  The
proceedings emanating from Case Crime No. 706/2024 registered
at P.S. Kalamassery are hereby quashed based on a settlement
between the parties.
4

--- Page 123 ---
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Criminal Appeal No(s).      /2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION 
 
TRANSFER PETITION (CIVIL) NO(S).970-971 OF 2026 
 
PRIYANSHU AMAREN                     ...PETITIONER (S) 
VERSUS  
NOOPUR                  ...RESPONDENT(S) 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. The present petitions have been filed by the petitioner -
husband seeking transfer of Matrimonial Case No. 426 of 
2021, instituted by the respondent -wife, and Matrimonial 
Case No. 73 of 2023, instituted by the petitioner -husband, 
both pending before the Prin cipal Judge, Family Court, 
Patna, Bihar, to the Court of the Principal Judge, Family 
Court, New Delhi. 
2. The facts in brief are as follows:  
2.1 The marriage between the parties was solemnised on 
19th April 2019 in accordance with Hindu rites and 
customs. The parties have been residing separately 
since March 2020. 
2.2 The respondent -wife instituted Matrimonial Case No. 
426 of 2021 seeking dissolution of marriage, which is 
pending before the Family Court, Patna.  

--- Page 133 ---
T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  2 
 
2.3 The petitioner -husband thereafter instituted 
Matrimonial Case No. 73 of 2023 seeking restitution of 
conjugal rights. The said proceedings came to be 
transferred from Ranchi to Patna pursuant to the order 
dated 13th December, 2022 passed by this Court in 
Transfer Petition (Civil) No. 307 of 2022. 
2.4 Both parties are presently residing in New Delhi and 
jointly seek transfer of the aforesaid proceedings to 
Delhi. 
3. We have learned counsel for the parties and perused the 
material available on the record.  
4. During the pendency of these petitions, this Court, vide order 
dated 21st  May, 2026, referred the disputes between the 
parties to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre. The parties 
have, pursuant thereto, arrived at a Settlement Agreement 
dated 15th June, 2026. 
5. A joint application, being I.A. No. 216314 of 2026, has been 
filed under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, seeking 
appropriate orders to give effect to the Settlement Agreement, 
including dissolution of the marriage and closure of all 
pending proceedings arising out of the matrimonial dispute. 
6. We have perused the Settlement Agreement and have 
interacted with the parties. They have affirmed before us that 

--- Page 134 ---
T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  3 
 
the settlement has been arrived at voluntarily, of their own 
free will and without any coercion, undue influence or fraud. 
They have further stated that there is no possibility of 
reconciliation and have mutually agreed to dissolve their 
marriage. 
7. As per the terms of the Settlement Agreement, the parties 
have agreed to withdraw all proceedings instituted by them 
against each other and have waived all claims towards 
permanent alimony, interim maintenance or any other 
financial support from each other . They have also 
undertaken not to raise any further claims or initiate any 
civil or criminal proceedings against each other in relation to 
the matrimonial dispute. 
8. We are satisfied that the Settlement Agreement has been 
voluntarily executed by the parties and that its terms are 
lawful. Having regard to the amicable resolution of all 
disputes through mediation before the Supreme Court 
Mediation Centre and the unequivo cal desire of the parties 
to bring their matrimonial relationship to an end, we are of 
the considered view that this is a fit case for exercise of the 
plenary powers of this Court under Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India to do complete justice betwee n the 
parties and bring a quietus to all disputes arising out of their 
matrimonial relationship. 

--- Page 135 ---
T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  4 
 
9. Accordingly, I.A. No. 216314 of 2026 is allowed. In terms of 
the Settlement Agreement which shall form part of this order 
and in exercise of our powers under Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India, we issue the following directions: 
9.1. The marriage solemnised between the petitioner and 
the respondent on 19th April, 2019 stands dissolved 
by a decree of divorce by mutual consent. 
9.2.  All pending civil and criminal proceedings instituted 
by either party against the other, arising out of or in 
connection with their matrimonial dispute, shall 
stand quashed and shall be deemed to have been 
finally disposed of. This shall include, inter alia: 
(i) Criminal Complaint Case bearing CCC(P) No.1177 
of 2021 pending before the CJM, Patna Sadar, 
Patna, Bihar 
(ii) Matrimonial Case No.426 of 2021 pending before 
Principal Judge, Family Court, Patna, Bihar. 
(iii) Matrimonial Case No.73 of 2023 pending before 
Principal Judge, Family Court, Patna, Bihar. 
10. Both parties, who are present before this Court, have 
affirmed that they shall abide by the terms and conditions of 
the Settlement Agreement and shall not raise any further 

--- Page 136 ---
T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  5 
 
claims or initiate any civil or criminal proceedings against 
each other in relation to the matrimonial dispute. 
11. The transfer petitions stand disposed of in the aforesaid 
terms. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
Registry shall communicate this order to all the concerned 
Courts where the matters were pending and have been 
closed by this order. Formal orders may be passed by the 
respective Courts closing the proceedings. The Registry shall 
also draw the decree accordingly. 
 
……………………………..J. 
[VIKRAM NATH]

[SANDEEP MEHTA]

Learned Amicus Curiae  has placed his note dated
06.10.2026 with regard to the status of the progress on
the directions issued by this Court and also with
respect  to  the  extent  noted  in  the  order  dated
23.09.2026. The said note is taken on record.
We are not commenting on the note of the learned
Amicus  Curiae . However, we direct the three States
(Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) to file
their further compliance affidavit(s) on the directions
issued by this Court in the previous orders dated
26.05.2026 and 22.07.2026, within two weeks from today,
and to serve a copy thereof upon the learned  Amicus
Curiae. Learned Amicus Curiae shall thereafter have one
week’s time to collate the contents of the affidavit(s)
and submit a fresh note/report by the next date.
Learned  Amicus  Curiae has also brought to the
notice of the Court that incidents of violence with the
forest officials and the incidents of rampant illegal
mining ought to be informed to this Court by the
concerned State Government officials.
It was submitted that the information pertaining
to these incidents percolates down to the Amicus from
SMWP(C)NO.2/2026 etc.
4

--- Page 142 ---
different sources after some delay and thus, it becomes
very difficult for him to apprise the Court of these
happenings.
Considering the above submissions of learned
Amicus  Curiae, we hereby provide that the editors of
the newspapers in which these incidents are reported
would be at liberty to forthwith send the copies of the
news reports to the AOR, Ms. Rupali Samuel at email
address ‘advocaterupalisamuel@gmail.com’ and the CEC at
email  address  ‘ cecindia202gmail.com’.  Upon  such
information being received, it would be open for the
Amicus Curiae  to apprise the Court of these happenings
so that suitable directions can be issued.

Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.)  No.18378/2026
[Arising  out  of  impugned  final  judgment  and  order  dated
21-07-2026 in IA No. 7740/2026 passed by the High Court of
Jharkhand at Ranchi]
SAGAR SAHU                                         Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND                             Respondent(s)
FOR ADMISSION 
IA No. 295977/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 06-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Sanjeev Kumar, Sr. Adv.
Ms. Manjula Gupta- 1043, AOR
                   Ms. Manjula Gupta, Adv.
                   Mr. Sudir Kumar Santoshi, Adv.
                   Mr. Prem Sunder Jha, Adv.
                   
                   
For Respondent(s) : Mr. Shantanu Sagar, AOR
Mr. Anil Kumar, Adv.
SLP(Crl.)  No.18378/2026 1

--- Page 151 ---
Mr. Abhishek Kumar Gupta, Adv.
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The Petitioner was convicted and sentenced to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for life by the Trial Court for
offences under Sections 302/34 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (for short, “IPC”), in connection with FIR
No. 83 of 2019 registered at P.S. Lohardaga. The appeal
against conviction is pending before the High Court.
Vide the impugned order, the High Court declined to
grant bail to the Petitioner during the pendency of the
appeal against his conviction before the High Court.
The Petitioner seeks suspension of his sentence and
release on bail pending final disposal of his appeal
against conviction before the High Court.
2. It is alleged that the Petitioner committed the murder
of his wife, Pratima, and one Ganesh Singh at the
Petitioner’s house, thereafter locked the house and
fled from the spot. The alleged motive for the murders
was the purported illicit relationship between the two
SLP(Crl.)  No.18378/2026 2

--- Page 152 ---
deceased, on account of which a Panchayat had also been
convened about three months prior to the incident.
3. The Trial Court convicted the Petitioner holding that
the prosecution has established a complete chain of
circumstantial  evidence.  The  Court  noted  that  the
bodies of the deceased were found from the house of the
Petitioner, and that medical evidence and prosecution
witnesses established that the death was homicidal, and
motivated. 
4. The High Court, vide the impugned order, declined to
grant  bail  to  the  Petitioner  holding  that  the
circumstances  projected  by  the  prosecution  clearly
indicate  that  it  was  the  Petitioner  who  was
instrumental in committing the alleged murder.
5. Learned Counsel for the Petitioner submitted that it
was the Petitioner himself who informed the Police
about the dead bodies found in his house, but no FIR
was registered at that stage. Thereafter, when the
Police visited the Petitioner’s house to inspect the
scene, the Petitioner, who had informed the Police
about the incident, was not taken along with them. It
SLP(Crl.)  No.18378/2026 3

--- Page 153 ---
was further submitted that the lock and key allegedly
used by the Police to open and enter the Petitioner’s
house were neither seized nor produced before Court. It
was also submitted that no weapon was recovered or
alleged to have been used in the commission of the
offence  and,  therefore,  it  was  improbable  for  the
Petitioner to have committed the murder of two adult
persons. It is also submitted that the Petitioner has
no  criminal  antecedents  and  has  already  undergone
custody for over one year and two months. Without
prejudice, it is also submitted that the paramour of
the petitioner’s wife was found in his house and there
cannot be any premeditation alleged on the petitioner
if at all he is found guilty of the crime.
6. Taking a holistic view, we suspend the sentence imposed
on the petitioner and order that the petitioner be
released on bail forthwith, if not required in any
other case, subject to terms and conditions that the
Court of Sessions Judge, Lohardaga, may deem fit to
impose, pending the final disposal of his appeal before
the High Court.
SLP(Crl.)  No.18378/2026 4

--- Page 154 ---
7. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition
is disposed of.
8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.
(CHANDRESH)                                     (POOJA SHARMA)

MAZHARUL ISLAM                                     Petitioner(s)

CERTIFICATE

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Maruf Khan, Sr. Adv.

                   Mr. Durgesh Ramchandra Gupta- 3582, AOR
                   
                   
For Respondent(s) : Ms. Ruchira Goel, Adv.
Diary No.49818/2026 1

--- Page 156 ---
Ms Rishik Rishabh, Adv.
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The Petitioner was convicted and sentenced to seven years
of rigorous imprisonment by the Trial Court for offences under
Sections 147, 148, 304/149, 308/149, 323/149, 325/149 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, “IPC”), in connection with
FIR No. 162 of 2004 registered at P.S. Khetasarai, Jaunpur. The
appeal against conviction is pending before the High Court. Vide
the impugned order, the High Court suspended the sentences of
the co-accused, Rashid and Bablu, while declining to suspend the
sentence imposed upon the Petitioner. The Petitioner seeks
suspension of his sentence and release on bail pending final
disposal of his appeal against conviction before the High Court.
3. It is alleged that the Petitioner, along with four others
armed  with  iron  rods,  sticks  and  lathis,  attacked  the
complainant’s  father.  The  specific  allegation  against  the
Petitioner is that he struck the complainant’s father on the
Diary No.49818/2026 2

--- Page 157 ---
head with a bamboo stick, resulting in his death. It is further
alleged that when the complainant and his brothers intervened,
they too were assaulted.
4. The Trial Court convicted the Petitioner and the other
accused, holding that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses,
corroborated  by  the  medical  evidence,  established  the
prosecution case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
5. The High Court, vide the impugned order, declined to
suspend the sentence imposed upon the Petitioner, principally on
the ground that the fatal blow was specifically attributed to
him and that he has four criminal antecedents.
6. Learned Counsel for the Petitioner submitted that both
parties sustained injuries during the incident and that the
Petitioner himself suffered three simple injuries. A cross-case
was also lodged from the side of the accused vide FIR No. 162A
of 2004, in which the members of the complainant’s party were
convicted under Sections 147 and 323/149 of the IPC. It was
further submitted that the alleged criminal antecedents are
merely cases registered and have not resulted in convictions. It
Diary No.49818/2026 3

--- Page 158 ---
was lastly submitted that the Petitioner remained on bail
throughout the twenty-year trial without any allegation of
misuse of the liberty of bail. Following his conviction, he has
been in custody for over one year and eight months and the
appeal against conviction pending before the High Court is
likely to take considerable time for final disposal.
7. Considering that the co-accused, who have been convicted
and  sentenced  for  the  same  offences,  have  been  granted
suspension of sentence, and that the Petitioner and other
accused had also sustained injuries in the incident, while the
complainant’s side stands convicted in the cross-case arising
from the same incident, we are of the view that the sentence
imposed upon the Petitioner can also be suspended.
8. Taking a holistic view, we suspend the sentence imposed on
the petitioner and order that the petitioner be released on bail
forthwith, if not required in any other case, subject to terms
and conditions that the First Additional Sessions Judge’s Court,
Jaunpur, may deem fit to impose, pending the final disposal of
his appeal before the High Court. 
Diary No.49818/2026 4

--- Page 159 ---
9. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

view of a video on Instagram.   The fact
remains that the appellants, who are husband
and  wife,  have  joined  the  investigation
pursuant to our order dated 03.08.2026. 
The facts would indicate that there was
a  dispute  which  emanated  between  the
appellants  and  the  purported  deceased
pursuant to his removal from the partnership.
Considering the aforesaid circumstances,
we are inclined to have a prima  facie view,
only for the purpose of deciding the present
appeal that the rigour of Section 306 of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  pari  materia  to
Section 108 of the BNS, may not get attracted
in facts of the present case.

--- Page 167 ---
3
Considering the above, we are inclined
to grant anticipatory bail to the appellants.
However,  we  make  it  clear  that  the
aforesaid observations made by us shall not
have  any  bearing  on  the  subsequent
proceedings. 
Accordingly, the impugned order stands
set  aside  and  the  appellants  are  granted
anticipatory  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions subject to the satisfaction of the
concerned Trial Court.
The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall
stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 4764 OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.18324 of 2026)
Francis Arun @ Kiran Chandrasekar
& Anr. ...Appellants
Versus
State of Tamil Nadu         ...Respondent
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. Exemption application allowed.
3. The present petition arises out of the impugned final judgment
and order dated 05.06.2026 passed by the Hon’ble High Court of
Judicature at Madras in CRL OP No. 13764 of 2026. By the impugned
order, the High Court directed the Ld. Chief Judicial Magistrate,
Coimbatore to accept the sureties furnished by the appellants
(Accused Nos. 3 and 5 in C.C. No. 144 of 2012) subject to the
condition that each appellant deposit a sum of Rs. 5,00,000/- on the
date of re-submission of the sureties and pay the balance fine
amount on or before 01.09.2026, failing which they were to be
secured to undergo the remaining sentence. 
4. Briefly stated, the appellants were convicted by the Ld. Chief
Judicial Magistrate, Coimbatore in C.C. No. 144 of 2012 vide
1

--- Page 176 ---
judgment dated 26.03.2026 for offences under Sections 120-B read
with 468, 471, 420 IPC and Sections 420, 468, 471, 419 IPC, and
sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a total consecutive period of
14 years along with a cumulative fine of Rs. 15,00,000/- each. 
5.  Aggrieved by the conviction, the appellants filed Criminal
Appeal No. 253 of 2026 before the Ld. Principal District and Sessions
Judge, Coimbatore, along with Crl. M.P. No.1 of 2026 for suspension
of sentence. By order dated 30.04.2026, the Appellate Court
suspended the substantive sentence of imprisonment pending
appeal and ordered their release on bail upon executing a bond for
Rs. 10,000/- each with two sureties for a like sum each to the
satisfaction  of  the  Ld.  Chief  Judicial  Magistrate,  Coimbatore,
alongside reporting conditions. 
6. Upon the appellants submitting their sureties on 05.05.2026,
the trial court returned the surety memo on the ground that only the
substantive sentence of imprisonment had been suspended, the fine
had not been paid, and consequently the default sentence remained
in operation. The appellants then approached the High Court under
Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
(BNSS). The High Court, while allowing the petition, imposed
onerous monetary conditions requiring immediate deposit of Rs.
5,00,000/- each and full payment of fine by 01.09.2026.
2

--- Page 177 ---
7. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the appellants
and the learned counsel representing the State.
8. Having perused the materials on record, it is noted that the
appellants remained on bail throughout the trial and there is no
allegation  of  misusing  their  liberty  or  absconding.  Once  the
Appellate Court exercises its jurisdiction under Section 430 BNSS
and suspends the substantive sentence of imprisonment pending
statutory  appeal,  imposing  heavy  pre-  conditions  of  onerous
monetary deposits for releasing the accused on bail or enforcing
default  sentences  during  appeal  pendency  defeats  the  very
objective of suspending the sentence. 
9. In view of the above facts and circumstances, the impugned
judgment and order dated 05.06.2026 passed by the High Court in
CRL OP No. 13764 of 2026 is hereby set aside. 
10. The appellants (Francis Arun @ Kiran Chandrasekar and Asha
Sharlet @ Priya Dharmaraj) are ordered to be released on regular
bail during the pendency of Criminal Appeal No. 253 of 2026 before
the Appellate Court, subject to the terms and conditions that the
trial court may deem fit and proper to impose.
11. The appeal is disposed of.
3

--- Page 178 ---
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

115(2),  64(1),  352  and  3(5)  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
6. Allegation  against  the  appellant  is  that  taking
advantage of the absence of his brother, who works in the
State of Sikkim, he committed ‘rape’ on his brother’s
wife.
7. This Court, by order dated 31.08.2026, had issued
notice and granted interim protection to the appellant
subject  to  the  appellant  co-operating  with  the
investigation.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that there
are serious disputes between the two brothers and the
related accusations are a fallout of such disputes. He
submits that the allegation of committing ‘rape’ by the
appellant on his own sister-in-law is utterly false. He
submits that though this Court had directed the appellant
to co-operate with the investigation, the police had
completed the investigation by then, whereafter final
report was submitted.
9. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar, on
the other hand, submits that investigation disclosed the
accusations to be false. Therefore, prosecution filed a
closure report. The Magistrate did not accept the final
report and issued summons to the appellant. Since the
appellant did not respond to the summons, Bailable Warrant
of Arrest was issued, followed by Non-Bailable Warrant of
2

--- Page 192 ---
Arrest. In the meanwhile, the prayer for anticipatory bail
made by the appellant was rejected by the High Court.
10. Learned counsel for Respondent No.2-informant submits
that merely because prosecution had submitted a closure
report,  would  not  exonerate  the  appellant  from  the
offence. The Trial Court has considered all aspects of the
matter and has refused to accept the closure report. When
summons have been issued to the appellant, he did not
appear. In such circumstances, he submits that the benefit
of  pre-arrest  bail  should  not  be  extended  to  the
appellant.
11. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court. We have
also carefully perused the materials on record.
12. While it is true that once the prosecution filed the
closure report, the need and necessity for obtaining
anticipatory  bail  by  the  accused  would  not  survive,
nonetheless, we find that the Trial Court has not accepted
the closure report and has decided to proceed with the
trial. In such circumstances, we are of the view that the
benefit  of  pre-arrest  bail  may  be  extended  to  the
appellant.
13. That being the position, we set aside the impugned
order dated 24.06.2026 passed by the High Court and make
our  order  dated  31.08.2026  absolute,  subject  to  the
condition that appellant shall appear before the Trial
Court within 07 days from today and submit his bail bonds
3

--- Page 193 ---
to  the  satisfaction  of  the  Trial  Court.  He  shall
thereafter appear before the Trial Court on the dates
fixed for the trial and not seek unnecessary adjournments.
14. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s).           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) Nos.14620/2026)
VISHNU DAS VAISHNAV      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Himachal
Pradesh.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 26.02.2026
passed by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is an accused in FIR No.213/2024 registered
at Police Station- Una Sadar, District- Una, Himachal
Pradesh under Sections 15 and 29 of the Narcotics Drugs
and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS
Act’).
5. Allegation  against  the  appellant  is  that  upon
interception of a truck by the police at Una, 05 sacks
1

--- Page 196 ---
containing 01 quintal, 46 kgs and 890 grams of poppy husk
were recovered. The truck was driven by one Rahul Sharma.
During investigation, Rahul Sharma disclosed that he had
procured the contraband from the appellant and 90 kgs
thereof  was  meant  for  one  Gaurav  Sharma,  who  was
subsequently named as an accused in the case.
6. Appellant was arrested on 26.09.2025 and has been in
custody since then.
7. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
27.07.2026, pursuant to which respondent-State of Himachal
Pradesh has filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that no
recovery was made, either from the person of the appellant
or from the residential or business premises of the
appellant. Merely on the confessional statement of accused
Rahul Sharma, appellant has been implicated in this case.
He  has  already  spent  more  than  a  year  in  custody.
Regarding trial, he submits that prosecution has cited 32
witnesses, out of which only 06 have been examined;
therefore,  trial  will  take  its  own  time.  In  such
circumstances, he seeks bail for the appellant.
9. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-State
of Himachal Pradesh has referred to the counter-affidavit
filed by the respondent-State of Himachal Pradesh and
submits that various amounts were credited in the bank
account  of  the  appellant.  These  sums  of  money  were
provided to the appellant by co-accused Gaurav Sharma.
2

--- Page 197 ---
Therefore, the link of the appellant becomes quite clear.
She further submits that appellant is an accused in an
earlier criminal case, also concerning NDPS. He is a
habitual offender and, therefore, it would not be prudent
to enlarge him on bail, at this stage.
10. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
11. While it is true that there have been transactions in
the bank account of the appellant with amounts provided by
Gaurav Sharma, a co-accused, as of now other than the
confessional statement of co-accused Rahul Sharma, prima
facie there is no incriminating material to implicate the
appellant in the offence. Though the quantity of poppy
husk seized is much above the commercial quantity, the
same was seized from the truck driven by co-accused Rahul
Sharma. Appellant has already undergone more than a year
in custody. In the trial, 26 more prosecution witnesses
have to be examined. Therefore, the trial will take its
own time. In such circumstances, balancing the interest
between the parties, we are inclined to grant bail to the
appellant.
12. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
26.02.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
13. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the jurisdictional Special Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall
be released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
3

--- Page 198 ---
deemed appropriate.
14. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

was referred to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre to explore
the possibility of a settlement between the parties.
3. Learned counsel for the respective parties submitted that
a Settlement Agreement has been arrived at and acted upon by
the  respective  parties.  The  Settlement  Agreement  dated

1

--- Page 201 ---
4. Learned counsel for the respective parties submitted that
taking on record the Settlement Agreement as well as the joint
application, the marriage between the parties may be dissolved
by a decree of divorce by mutual consent. Consequently, the
Transfer Petition may be disposed of.
5. The parties are present before this Court. The petitioner
has  appeared  in-person  while  the  respondent  has  appeared
through video conferencing facility. The parties have been
identified by their respective counsel. 
6. When queried by this Court, they stated that they have
indeed arrived at a settlement of all their disputes which are
crystallized in the form of terms and conditions in the
Settlement  Agreement  arrived  at  before  the  Supreme  Court
Mediation Centre and that they have decided to part ways by
seeking dissolution of their marriage by a decree of divorce by
mutual consent on the terms and conditions stated in the
Settlement agreement. They have also filed a joint application
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India seeking divorce.
7. The parties also stated that they have arrived at a
settlement on their own free volition without there being any
coercion or undue influence from any side. They also stated
that they would abide by the terms and conditions of the
Settlement Agreement.
8. In the above backdrop, we have taken on record the
Settlement Agreement dated 16.06.2025 as well as the joint
application filed by the parties under Article 142 of the
2

--- Page 202 ---

factory to be transferred to accounts held by him, his wife,
close relatives and other persons who had not supplied sugarcane
to  the  factory.  The  audit  report  quantifies  the  disputed
transactions at approximately Rs.1.91 crore.

delete an existing account or independently authorize payment.

and the concerned banks. It was argued that a large cooperative
sugar factory could not have remained dependent upon a single
Assistant Accountant and that a diversion continuing for nearly
six years could not have escaped the annual audit and scrutiny
of superior officers, and that the Petitioner has been made a
scapegoat.  It  was  further  submitted  that  investigation  is
complete and other accused have either secured bail or interim
protection.
4. On a prima facie consideration of the material on record
and after hearing the learned counsel for the parties, we are of
the opinion that the petitioner can be released on bail, on such
terms and conditions that the Judicial First Class Magistrate’s
Court, Rahata (the jurisdictional court) may deem fit and
appropriate to impose. The petitioner shall appear before the

...Appellant

State of NCT of Delhi     
...Respondent
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. This appeal seeks setting aside of the impugned order dated
06.08.2026 passed by the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi in Bail
Application No. 2666 of 2026, whereby the High Court declined to
grant anticipatory bail to the appellant in connection with FIR No.
0287/2026 registered at Police Station New Usmanpur, Delhi, for
offences punishable under Sections 80, 85, and 3(5) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS). 
3. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the appellant
has already joined the investigation and was granted interim
protection against coercive action by the learned Sessions Court
vide order dated 05.06.2026. All other co-accused persons, namely
Bhagwat  Prasad  (father-in-law),  Pushpa  Devi  (mother-in-law),

--- Page 244 ---
2
Praveen Kumar (brother-in-law), and Anju Kumari (sister-in-law)—
arising from the same FIR have already been granted anticipatory
bail.
4. Learned  Additional  Solicitor  General  appearing  for  the
Respondent State and learned counsel for the Complainant has
opposed the grant of anticipatory bail.
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material available on record, it is an admitted position that the
appellant has joined the investigation. The initial statements
recorded during inquest proceedings before the SDM did not contain
specific allegations of dowry harassment. Co-accused persons
similarly situated with omnibus allegations have already been
granted anticipatory bail.
6. Without expressing any opinion on the merits of the allegations
or the ongoing investigation, since all the co-accused have already
been granted anticipatory bail, on parity, this Court is inclined to
grant anticipatory bail to the appellant.
7. It is accordingly ordered that in the event of arrest of the
appellant (Ravi Kumar) in connection with FIR No. 0287/2026, Police
Station New Usmanpur, Delhi, he shall be released on bail subject to
conditions the I.O. may deem fit to impose, on condition also of

--- Page 245 ---
3
continued cooperation in the investigation.
8. Once the appellant is released on bail by the I.O., on directions
issued by the I.O. or summons issued by the jurisdictional court, the
appellant shall appear before the jurisdictional court and furnish bail
bonds and ensure due appearance in the trial.
9. The appeal is allowed.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The present petition challenges the interim orders dated 27.04.2026
and 01.07.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna in Cr.
Misc. No. 10883 of 2026. By the order dated 27.04.2026, the High Court
directed  the  parties  to  explore  an  amicable  settlement  or,  in  the
alternative,  required  the  appellant  to  consider  compensating  the
Informant for the value of the disputed land. Subsequently, vide order
dated 01.07.2026, the High Court directed the Senior Superintendent of
Police, Patna, to ensure the personal presence of the parties in Chambers.
3. The present case arises out of Phulwari Sharif P.S. Case No. 1390 of
2025, registered under Sections 316(2), 318(4), 319(2), 336(2), 336(3),
337, 338, 131, 61(2), and 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023.
4. It is contended by the learned counsel for the appellant that he is a
builder who entered into a Development Agreement dated 29.03.2022
with the co-accused (Jahan Ara). The underlying disputes regarding title
over  the  subject  property  (Khata  No.  1065,  Plot  Nos.  1718  &  1719,
1

--- Page 248 ---
measuring 6 decimals in Phulwari Sharif, Patna) are primarily between the
co-accused and the Informant's husband, in respect of which Title Suit No.
161/2025  is  already  pending  before  the  Civil  Judge  (Senior Division),
Patna. 
5. Learned counsel appearing for the State of Bihar and the Informant
have opposed the grant of anticipatory bail.
6. Considering the nature of the allegations, the civil genesis of the
dispute,  and  the  fact  that  the  appellant  has  no  relevant  criminal
antecedents, we are inclined to allow pre-arrest bail to the appellant.
7. Accordingly, the impugned orders dated 27.04.2026 and 01.07.2026
passed by the High Court of Patna in Cr. Misc. No. 10883 of 2026 are set
aside.
8. It is ordered that in the event of arrest or surrender of the appellant
(Sultan Ahmed) in connection with Phulwari Sharif P.S. Case No. 1390 of
2025, he shall be released on anticipatory bail, subject to the conditions
the  I.O.  may  deem  fit  to  impose,  on  condition  also  of  continued
cooperation in the investigation.
9. Once the appellant is released on bail by the I.O., on directions
issued by the I.O. or summons issued by the jurisdictional court, the
appellant  shall  appear before  the  jurisdictional court  and furnish bail
bonds and ensure due appearance in the trial.
10. The appeals are allowed.
